title: The Gleaner's Handful
hookLine: a gleaner's family gives away its last barley, and a school of atoms opens with the same word: dharma
carry: even a school of atoms begins with dharma
tomorrow: a father tells his son to break a seed. what's inside?

lines: NOT WORTH A HANDFUL OF BARLEY.
cards: After the great war, King Yudhishthira holds a horse sacrifice so lavish that everyone says nothing like it has ever been seen. Then, in the middle of all the praise, a mongoose crawls out of a hole.
Half its body is gold. And it speaks: this whole sacrifice, it says, isn't worth a little barley flour that a poor gleaner once gave away in Kurukshetra.

teach.h: THE GLEANER GIVES HIS LAST BARLEY.
teach.b: This is from the Mahabharata. The gleaner lived by unchha: picking up the grains left in the fields after harvest, one by one. In a famine, he, his wife, his son and his son's wife scraped together a little barley.
Just as they sat to eat, a hungry guest arrived. The gleaner gave him his share. The guest was still hungry.
His wife gave hers, then the son, then the son's wife.
Then the guest revealed who he was: Dharma himself. The mongoose had rolled in the flour left on the floor, and half of it turned gold.
Ever since, it has gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, looking for one great enough to gild the other half.

Now today's school, Vaisheshika, credited to a sage named Kanada. Tradition says his name comes from living like that gleaner, on grains, kana, gathered one by one. Whether or not that's history, his book fits it.
You'd expect a school of atoms to open with matter.
The Vaisheshika Sutra opens with dharma: now we will explain dharma, that from which come rising in this world and the highest good. Before it counts a single particle, it says why counting matters.

And tradition links its name to vishesha, particularity: what makes each thing this one and not another. So the teaching, plainly: for this Hindu school, knowing what the world is made of serves dharma.
Put the gleaner beside it, and here's our reading: dharma is done in particulars. This grain, this guest, this handful. The gleaner's gift wasn't big.
It was given. Today, the particular thing in front of you counts.

how: Vaisheshika is studied with Nyaya, often as one joined system, through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries; in many Hindu homes food is offered before it's eaten and treated as too sacred to waste.

o: the school that holds each thing is particular
a set of rules for dividing a family's land
a rite for blessing the first harvest grain

games.q: a gleaner and a grain-gatherer — tap the pairs.
p: the sage linked to gathering grains

s: the Vaisheshika Sutra opens with atoms
it opens with dharma: that from which come rising in this world and the highest good.
the mongoose said the king's sacrifice outweighed the gleaner's barley
the other way round: a handful given by a starving family was worth more.
tradition links the name Vaisheshika to vishesha, particularity
what makes each thing this one, not another.

games.q: you're writing a book that will list everything the world is made of. by Kanada's example, what goes in the very first line?
games.why: the Vaisheshika Sutra begins: now we will explain dharma. the knowing serves a good life and the highest good.

practice: Before your next meal, take one grain of rice, or one crumb, and really look at it: someone grew it, someone carried it, it's this one.
Many Hindus offer food before eating, and some say a verse from the Gita, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman. If you pray, offer the meal that way, or in your own words.
If you don't, say a quiet thank-you for this particular plate.

wordCard.voice: Vaisheshika. The school of Kanada, linked by tradition to vishesha, particularity, and known for its atoms. Its sutra opens with dharma.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Vaisheshika, the school whose name tradition links to vishesha, particularity.

carryVoice: Your line: even a school of atoms begins with dharma. A gleaner's handful outweighed a king's sacrifice. See you tomorrow.
